title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard/scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; n_11 = 400; n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work demonstrates that LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings, while separate lines of work on verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers show that post‑generation checks reduce syntactic and semantic errors in infrastructure‑as‑code and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes?

Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks.

Contributions and high‑level finding. We (1) preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1; (2) report artifact‑grounded confirmatory results that show universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); and (3) provide a diagnostic, artifact‑grounded analysis that the preregistered shared_generation semantics combined with reuse of a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run. We conclude with concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations based on archived traces.
sections.related_work: This study intersects several threads relevant to LLMs for NetOps: (1) intent→configuration generation, where recent work shows LLMs can synthesize usable configuration artifacts in controlled benchmarks and testbeds (e.g., intent‑to‑configuration translations and PreConfig approaches) but typically evaluates generation quality rather than staged rollout safety [1,2,3]; (2) verifier‑guided IaC workflows (e.g., verifier‑guided model fine‑tuning and policy‑guided repair) that report correctness gains in provisioning and IaC domains and motivate runtime verifier integration for NetOps [4,5]; (3) deterministic network verification and reachability tools that effectively detect configuration errors in offline/emulated settings while differing in scope and network model assumptions [6,7]; and (4) agentic and tool‑augmented LLM systems (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestration) applied to AIOps/RCA tasks that improve capability but introduce operational failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, miscalibrated confidence) and thus motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments [8]. Surveys and reviews repeatedly highlight an evaluation gap: standardized, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to directly probe verifier utility under those constraints.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. We preregistered the study under cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1. The primary confirmatory estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test was produced for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics and shared generation (construct validity note). Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Critically, the preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation that was delivered identically to both the baseline and guarded episodes. We explicitly note here (as required by the peer review) that this preregistered choice, combined with reuse of deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and scorer, makes the preregistered primary estimand effectively untestable in any execution where the shared candidate satisfies the deterministic validator—because identical accepted candidates necessarily produce identical paired outcomes. We mirror this explicit statement in the Abstract for immediate reader clarity.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and (in the guarded episode) routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation using a deterministic rule set recorded in validator_trace entries. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; all repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before/after states, and final validity decisions were recorded in validator_trace. In this execution repair_applied = false across all episodes.

Task generation, difficulty metadata, and deterministic replay checks. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task record contains structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; reproducible simulator failures or nondeterministic replays would be flagged and excluded per the missingness_plan. In the executed run all three‑replay checks passed and no exclusions were applied (complete_pairs = 400). The full per‑task difficulty labels are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and available for aggregation by auditors.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The primary contingency counts were baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numbers are reproduced directly from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Repair and rollback observations. Across the 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. This explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both conditions necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes.

Representative worked example (artifact excerpt). A representative archived task (task‑000001) illustrates typical artifact content. The shared initial candidate (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) and both condition responses are identical:

interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30

interface edge1 admin up

The validator_trace for task‑000001 records parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false, demonstrating how an accepted shared candidate produces concordant accepted outcomes in both episodes.

Difficulty metadata availability and diversity note. The task manifest contains per‑task difficulty labels enabling stratified analyses; representative items in the archived manifest show a mix of medium, hard, and very_hard tasks (see representative entries). The complete per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 tasks are archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be deterministically aggregated by auditors. (The archived artifact bundle contains the full manifest and deterministic seeds required to reproduce such aggregates.)
sections.discussion:
Construct‑validity diagnosis. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings.

Consequences for power and inference. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference of ≈0.10 with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed deterministic ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply to these results. The exact p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the observed data under the preregistered design but cannot adjudicate whether a runtime guard would have improved outcomes under an alternative design that preserved generator variance.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations. Using archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete steps for future preregistered runs that preserve signal for generator×guard interactions (all recommendations derive from existing artifact fields and adapter semantics):

1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each arm receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has opportunities to accept, block, or request repair.

2) Distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to prevent conflation of runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; validator_trace entries show acceptance decisions and validation states and can be used to validate this separation.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding: preregister a reproducible fraction of perturbation seeds that increase baseline failure rates to preserve statistical power; task generator supports seed control and deterministic generation.

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling: ensure the benchmark composition includes a targeted fraction of very_hard tasks to produce measurable baseline errors; per‑task difficulty labels are archived for deterministic stratified sampling.

5) Instrument repair/rollback metrics as primary or secondary outcomes (repair_applied, repairs_requested, time‑to‑rollback) and log them in validator_trace and repair logs (already present in the artifacts) so future analyses can quantify guard action utility.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can hide the benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks that evaluate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve generator variance and independent adjudication as described above.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the numbers and traces reported here are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts produced by the run include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata, and the analysis results (paired contingency and bootstrap outputs). These artifacts contain the seeds, deterministic replay checks, and the validator_trace records that underpin the diagnosis and recommendations above; auditors can reproduce the reported summaries using the archived manifests and analysis code as recorded in the artifact bundle.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript reports representative sample counts to illustrate benchmark diversity but does not invent aggregated counts absent explicit artifact summarization in the manuscript body.
